theory.intro: Multiplying a whole number by $10$, $100$ or $1000$ moves each digit one, two or three places to a larger place value. Use a known multiplication fact first when multiplying by a multiple such as $30$ or $400$.
facts: For whole numbers, multiplying by $10$, $100$ or $1000$ puts one, two or three zeros after the number. The zeros hold the empty places.
Keep any zero already in the known product: $5 \times 800 = 40 \times 100 = 4000$. Two zeros are put after $40$.
steps: For a multiple of $10$, $100$ or $1000$, write it as a one-digit number times $10$, $100$ or $1000$.
Multiply that product by $10$, $100$ or $1000$, using place value.

workedExamples.question_text: Find (a) $9 \times 10$, (b) $9 \times 100$ and (c) $9 \times 1000$. Explain the place value of $9$ in each answer.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $9 \times 10=90$. The $9$ moves from ones to tens.
(b) $9 \times 100=900$. The $9$ moves from ones to hundreds.
(c) $9 \times 1000=9000$. The $9$ moves from ones to thousands.
The zeros hold the empty places.

$8 \times 7000$
$=8 \times 7 \times 1000$
$=56 \times 1000$
$=56000$
Multiplying $56$ by $1000$ puts three zeros after $56$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find $5 \times 800$ and $5 \times 8000$. Explain the zeros in the first answer and compare the two products.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$5 \times 800$
$=5 \times 8 \times 100$
$=40 \times 100$
$=4000$
The known product $40$ already ends in one zero. Multiplying by $100$ puts two more zeros after it.
$5 \times 8000$
$=5 \times 8 \times 1000$
$=40 \times 1000$
$=40000$
The second product is $10$ times the first, because $8000=10 \times 800$.

development.question_text: Rewrite $7 \times 80$ as a product using $8$ and $10$, then find the product.
Explain why $6 \times 700$ has two zeros after $42$.
development.solution_text:
$6 \times 700$
$=6 \times 7 \times 100$
$=42 \times 100$
$=4200$
The two zeros come from the factor $100$.

$4 \times 8000=32000$
$4 \times 800=3200$
The first product is $10$ times the second product.

mastery.question_text: Which is greater, $6 \times 400$ or $8 \times 300$, or are they equal?

A student writes $9 \times 800=720$.
Correct the calculation and explain the place-value error.
mastery.solution_text:
$9 \times 800$
$=9 \times 8 \times 100$
$=72 \times 100$
$=7200$
The student attached one zero instead of the two zeros from $800$.
